title: Tracing Eynan plaster sample 86-1 to Shelter 1
question: Did the burnt-lime sample analysed as 86-1 come from the plastered rim of Early Natufian Shelter 1 at Eynan-Mallaha, and what does the evidence establish about the feature's use?
summary: Shelter 1 is a plausible match for the bench-like feature described in the laboratory report. The excavation photograph and plan identify the shelter, and a published comparison explicitly proposes the match. The laboratory report traces the specimen to the Hebrew University collection through Ofer Bar-Yosef. The link between the collection specimen and the position sampled in the excavation is still missing.

steps.title: Locate Shelter 1 in the excavation record
steps.action: Compare the original November 1955 excavation photograph reproduced by the current field team with the phase-coded plan. Check the archived French titles for the same numbered feature.
steps.result: The archival photo labels portions of Shelter 1 on either side of Shelter 3. Its caption identifies Shelter 1's plastered perimeter, upright slabs, partly paved floor and square hearth. Haklay and Gopher place Shelter 1 near Cemetery A in Early Natufian Layer II, away from Shelters 131 and 51. The Nanterre archive uses abri n° 1, locus n° 1 and the early interpretation La grande tombe. JP557 also contains plates of Locus 3, so the dossier title alone does not identify the contents of an individual image.

steps.title: Follow Perrot's descriptions and illustrations
steps.action: Trace the first excavation interpretation, the 1966 feature description and the second Perrot reference used by the laboratory study. Compare the description with the plan and photos reproduced from the excavators' work.
steps.result: The current field team dates Perrot's first interpretation of the built complex as a monumental grave to his 1957 report in Antiquity and Survival. In 1966 he reconsidered the complex as superimposed dwellings. Perrot's p. 445, quoted by Dubreuil, describes a polished coating with red surviving inside a shallow circular depression about 5 m across. It extended over the edge as an outward-sloping rim, about 70 cm wide and bordered by upright stones. Goring-Morris and Belfer-Cohen reproduce a plan and photographs of the installation after Perrot (1966) and Perrot and Ladiray (1988). Kingery's other citation, Perrot's Mallaha (Eynan), 1975, discusses House 131, with a different plan and excavation photograph. The 1957 and 1966 full articles were not retrieved. The 1957 and 1966 archival dossiers identify where to inspect the original inked plans and the 1966 offprint.

steps.title: Read the laboratory label and collection credit
steps.action: Check the sample row, methods, institutional footnote and discussion in the 1988 laboratory report. Follow the named supplying collection and distinguish the published number from a field or museum identifier.
steps.result: Kingery, Vandiver and Prickett describe 86-1 as hard tan or brown material from an Eynan bench-like structure and interpret its microstructure and composition as incompletely calcined lime plaster altered after deposition. The footnote says it came from the Institute of Archaeology at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, courtesy of Ofer Bar-Yosef. It supplies no field or collection catalogue number, sampling point, locus, layer or collection date for 86-1. The Institute describes its collections and archives, but a public sample-level record or transfer slip for 86-1 was not located. Harvard's listed Bar-Yosef personal archive has accessions dated 1988–2008 and no pertinent file was identified. The Smithsonian's public laboratory finding aids identify institutional holdings with overlapping dates but do not establish custody of 86-1 or identify its receipt.

steps.title: Identify the missing field catalogue entry
steps.action: Look up the Perrot field catalogue, early notebooks, Shelter 1 drawings and photographic catalogue in the Nanterre finding aid. Check what can be inspected online.
steps.result: The strongest field lead is JP220, explicitly catalogued as containing a sample catalogue for 1955–1961. JP216 holds two notebooks from the 1955, 1956 and 1959 campaigns. JP553 contains original sections and drawings for loci 1, 26–29 and 51 and cross-references early records in JP220. JP557 plate 25 is catalogued as Locus 1. The archive lists 40 digitized slides for the 1955 campaign under JP646, EM_dia_1955_01 through EM_dia_1955_40. The contents of the JP220 sample catalogue and the original JP553 drawings were not available in the copies retrieved. The published Figure 4 is an accessible reproduction of a 1955 field photo, credited to JP646–JP659 as a group.

steps.title: Test whether the descriptions identify the same sample
steps.action: Compare the excavator's rim, the laboratory description and later analyses of other material at Eynan. Check whether any independent report gives a numbered sampling position for 86-1.
steps.result: Dubreuil explicitly argues that the feature analysed by Kingery and colleagues probably corresponds to Perrot's margelle. This is a published comparison of the descriptions. Kingery's sample row gives no arc dimensions, upright stones, red finish or other field marker that singles out the specimen's sampling spot. Valla and colleagues analysed other Eynan lime material, including flat pieces lining Locus 239 under Shelter 26, in separate samples documented in table 5. The Raman and micromorphology study by Es Sebar and colleagues distinguished lime plaster from other carbonate-rich material at the site, including geological and later-precipitated calcite. Neither study identifies or retests 86-1.

steps.title: Assess use independently of specimen identity
steps.action: Compare the publication sequence with the excavation team's current interpretation of the architecture, its relation to graves and documented modern disturbance.
steps.result: The construction and plastered perimeter are visible in the documented feature. The modern cut had already removed part of Shelter 1. The field team describes a disputed sequence and still considers the relation of the nested shelters to funerary activity open. A recovered sampling record could settle whether 86-1 dates to the Early Natufian context of Shelter 1. The historic function would still require evidence relating the bench, occupation surfaces and any burials by phase.

decision: Record this as a plausible descriptive match with unresolved specimen provenance. Keep the Early Natufian field observation at Shelter 1 separate from the laboratory identification of 86-1 at Eynan. The existing candidate link and provenance note cite the published comparison, the laboratory's collection credit and the archive finding aid. The specimen has no secure field date, and the question about the feature's use remains open.
next: Inspect the 1955–1961 sample catalogue in JP220 at MSH Mondes, using the Shelter 1 notebook, section or photograph to map any entry for the margelle or red enduit. Match its field number and sampling position to an original label, dispatch record or laboratory intake entry tied to 86-1 from the Hebrew University collection. If the number is absent, an annotated sampling photograph or a separately analysed surviving fragment with a drawing-based provenance could settle the material identification at Shelter 1. A new sample would have its own identity.
